answer: The super-channel comes first: the odu page states the pre-condition "Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added", and "The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created." Every facility carries managed-by (system or user, default system) and only user-created facilities can be user deleted. The odu class attribute confirms it: high-order is the top-most ODUCn/ODUk created by the system, everything else is low-order (default) or mapped. You then hand-add the low order ODUs, e.g. add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80, with odu-type ODUCn/ODUCni/ODU4/ODU4i/ODUflexi/ODUflex/ODU0/ODU1/ODU2/ODU2e. On a G40 line side the OTU is added against the flexo-group: add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1. flexo and flexo-group also default to managed-by system.

BERT is the bert command (Operational Mode only): bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10, plus bert stop/get/delete. test-signal-type is none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV or scrambled-idles; 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV, CarrierCTP monitors fec-frames. test-duration minimum 10 s, maximum 1000 hrs, 0 means indefinite; test-id is mandatory for stop. Test patterns are injected per facility via odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> (or ethernet) test-signal-type: none, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31, PRBS31_NONINV, with test-signal-direction ingress/egress/both and test-signal-monitoring true/false (default false). Loopback is the loopback attribute on otu, odu, ethernet and optical-carrier: none (default), facility (towards facility side) or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

Each end needs a secure-entity bound to the facility and pointed at the far end: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <facility> remote-secure-entity <AID>, where remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier (1830 GX G40), the remote ODU (G30) or the remote OTUFlex (CHM7/CHM7X L1 service encryption). enabled defaults to false so it must be set true; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited; re-key-frequency is 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800; re-key-fail-policy is kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic) and traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s, default 0. Certificates must already be in place: a local-certificate assigned to the secure-application (set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <cert>), the far end's peer-certificate (the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for L1 encryption), and the CA trusted-certificate chain, all loaded with import-certificate.

The telemetry object configures persistent and dynamic telemetry; it is system managed and cannot be manually deleted (show telemetry, set telemetry id <string>, length 0..4096). To see what is subscribed use show subscriptions for the list, then show current-subscription-<subscription-name>, which reports related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false) and user-access. What each one watches comes from show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<path-name>: subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in milliseconds (both default 0), and suppress-redundant (default true). For a target-defined stream with no sample-interval the system uses 10 seconds and raises a sub-10s heartbeat to 20 seconds.

At rest the database is encrypted: show db-protection-scheme reports encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode with 64-byte block size), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup / failed-on-bootup / disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which is changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before take-snapshot will run, the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption must be configured, either globally with set security-policies db-passphrase or passed inline as take-snapshot db-passphrase=***. It must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and special characters follow the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. take-snapshot then stores to db-instance temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback, with an optional description up to 128 characters; show database lists what exists.

Start at the configured route: show ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf> gives next-hop-address, interface, distance (1..255, default 1), advertised (default false), origin manual or dhcp, special-next-hop blackhole, and monitoring-state (unmonitored, ok, failed) with monitoring-instance. Whether it reached the forwarding table is show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>, which lists system routes from all sources and reports source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static) and special-next-hop none / blackhole / unreachable; for blackhole and unreachable routes no next-hop is created under the route. Which instance it landed in comes from show rib-<rib-name>, giving the vrf the RIB is bound to and its address-family, ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; each routing instance has one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> gives the resolved next-hop-address, show vrf-<name> the VRF type (mgmt or internal), and show routing the overall view.

The rejection comes from security-policies: strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum 8 characters, at least one lower case, one upper case, one number and one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password; with it disabled only a 1-character minimum applies. minimum-password-length is 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of any of the previous 5 passwords, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. The lockout comes from the user object: max-invalid-login is the maximum consecutive invalid login attempts before the account is suspended, range 0..255, default 5; suspension-time is 0..1440 minutes, default 5; user-status then shows lockout, and failed-logins resets to zero on a successful login. disable-user-lockout in security-policies overrides that behaviour. To clear the stuck session run show session to find the id, then kill-session <session-id> where the id has the form <ip-address>:<port>; you cannot kill your own session.

Local log files: number-of-files defaults to 10 with a range of 1..20 retained, and when rotating on max size the oldest files are discarded once the total exceeds that number; max-file-size defaults to 30 MB, range 1..30; source-facilities defaults to all, and by default severity is set to informational and above. The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Console logging is off by default: log-console enabled defaults to false. Remote servers default to enabled true, port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, message-coalescence true, source-facilities all, destination-facility-override disabled, sensitive-data none, origin manual. The single switch that kills everything remote is set syslog remote-logging-switch false (default true), which disables all remote logging destinations; syslog also carries log-relay (default false), log-file-message-coalescence (true), source-address (localhost), niap-compliant-logging and privacy-mode (both false).

What is raised now is show current-alarms, which gives number-of-alarms and last-changed (timestamp of the last raise or clear); show alarms or show alarm-<alarm-id> gives the detail, including perceived-severity, service-affecting, reported-time, alarm-category, corrective-action and operator-state. Manual clearing is clear [-f] alarm <alarm-type> [resource=...]; only the small subset of alarms with no automatic clear criteria can be cleared this way, and you list them with show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true. That mechanism applies only to system-wide/global alarms not associated with a particular resource. Whether inhibiting reporting drops what is already up is decided by set alarm-control arc-behavior: clear-alarms clears current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, while leave-alarms (the default) leaves them raised. alarm-control also carries alarm-soaking-behavior, automatic (default) or no-soak.

The dashboard is status equipment, which lists chassis, the cards per chassis with their subtype, the toms per card, and per-equipment temperature sensors and power values along with presence, oper-state and alarms, for example 'chassis-1 G42 (NC) temp 25C | power 2.1/4400 W' and 'card-1-1 XMM4 (Act) temp 25C'. To narrow it to one slot's chassis pass the chassis id as the filter, e.g. status equipment 5; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you get either all chassis or exactly one. For the raw sensor readings use show pm real-time data, which reports temperature (C) per card and per FANCTRL/PEM, inlet-temperature (C) on the chassis and fan-speed (percent) per FAN, with instant/avg/min/max columns. Physically it shows on the LEDs: show leds or show led status lists led-<location>/<name> with status off, green, flashing-green, yellow, amber, red, flashing-red, cycling (lamp test) or not-available, including entries such as led-1-2/chassis-major and led-1-FANCTRL-1/fault.

The line is the ots facility. show ots-<name> gives span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx, the measured span loss based on OSC including losses external to the fiber, range 0..99 dB where 99 dB means OLOS and which are only relevant when an OSC channel exists. span-loss-receive and span-loss-transmit are the user-configured fiber loss, 0..80 dB (rx also accepts 99 as not configured), default 0, and span-loss-reference selects which the system uses for automatic target OXcon powers: measured (default) or configured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80 dB or 99, default 99) is set autonomously, is persistent across boots, and in measured mode can be refreshed with the update command; span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0..10 dB, default 1.0. What the amplifier is compensating with is show amplifier-<name>: gain-operating versus gain-target (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual, input-power-mon and output-power-mon (-99..99 dBm), control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, span-loss-control (default enabled, and mandatory when span-loss-reference is measured), control-state (converged, fine-tuning, adjusting, stopped) and tilt-actual.

The chain is trib-ptp, the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver equipment and the immediate protocol layer, then the client facility itself (ethernet, fc, stm or a client otu), then a low-order odu (ODU4i, ODUflexi and so on) whose parent-odu points at the high-order ODUCn/ODUCni that the system created with the super-channel. The xcon ties the two ends together, e.g. add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1, and its network-mapping attribute names the server layer that supports it. Line side you then have otu (parent flexo-group), flexo/flexo-group, and line-ptp. The digital-to-optical handover sits at line-ptp / super-channel / optical-carrier: line-ptp carries service-type and line-system-mode openwave, described as the L1 to L0 local power control adjusting Tx power from the L1 transponder towards the L0 line-system card, and optical-carrier holds frequency, tx-power, modulation-format and baud-rate. From there it is pure L0: nmc, whose parent-facility is a Media Channel or an OMS, then oxcon, oms and ots.

No, they are two different objects. Counter crossing is PM: add or set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> low-threshold <v> high-threshold <v>, where the values are uint64/int64/decimal64, na or not-supported, default na. Whether a crossing is actually reported is the separate tca-supervision flag on set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>, with per-resource-type defaults from pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision and system limits from pm-threshold-profile. Changing how loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>, for example set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor, or set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>. The first creates the condition, the second re-grades a condition that already exists.

Stop the reporting with the alarm-report-control attribute: set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited, values allowed or inhibited. Note the card object documents its default as Inhibited, while the facilities on it (trib-ptp, odu, otu, ethernet, flexo, line-ptp, optical-carrier) default to allowed, so inhibit each facility you also want silent. You can additionally take the card out of service with set card-<name> admin-state maintenance (lock, unlock default, maintenance). What happens to the alarms it already raised is decided system-wide by set alarm-control arc-behavior: clear-alarms clears current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, while leave-alarms, the default, leaves them raised. So on a default node the existing alarms stay up and only new ones are suppressed; set arc-behavior clear-alarms first if you want the standing alarms to drop too.

Look at the secure-application: show secure-application-<id> [type] [active-certificate-id] [in-use] [status] [verify-client-cert]. active-certificate-id is the list of certificates assigned to that application and in-use (a leafref to active-certificate-id) is the one actually presented to the far end; type shows whether it acts as server or client and status shows enabled or disabled. Assign with set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY (multiple allowed). The identity itself is a local-certificate, the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing the secure application identity; show local-certificate-<id> gives status (valid, expired, revoked, untrusted, future, pending-import), trust-chain and used-by. Before it will come up you must import it with import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=<name> <PEM string> <passphrase>, plus the CA chain as trusted-certificate (root certificates must be installed individually) and, for L1 encryption, the far end's peer-certificate. For TLS mutual authentication set verify-client-cert to required (default disabled).

Pipe the PM output through the display filter: show pm <command flag> | display csv produces CSV data importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Narrow it to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter, for example show pm pm-15min, and filter further by AID, data-type, parameter, resource or resource-type; show pm <tab> lists every supported filter. Useful flags are -t for standard table format, -i=<chassis-name> to scope to one chassis (only once per command), -n=<number-of-records> for the maximum records per chassis (default 1000), -s=<skip-records> to page through, -st=/-et=<timestamp> in the form 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00, and -sbin/-ebin to bound the bins. Bin 0 is the current data and bins 1 to n are history; the NE stores 15min and 24h granularities.

Use show pm-catalog <string>, where the string is the catalog name. For example show pm-catalog parameter-undersized returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The equivalent per-parameter lookup is show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type], for example show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds, and plain show pm-parameter lists all of the pm parameters. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. A PM parameter identifier can be either a counter or a gauge, which is exactly what the type field tells you, and units gives the measurement unit.

Turn off data-supervision on that resource: set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false, for example set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false. data-supervision is the real-time data supervision flag for the resource, values true or false, default true. show pm-control displays the configuration for all currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The equivalent per-instance control is set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false, also true/false with a default of true. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, that is exactly what pm-control-entry is for: it configures PM for one particular resource, for one particular period, direction and location. Run set pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true, for example set pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na (default all) and location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end (default all); the same entry also carries data-supervision (true/false). show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> supported-parameters lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements.

Use show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]. The type field is either counter or gauge, and units is drawn from the enumeration na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors, MHz. For example show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized returns units packets and type counter. show pm-parameter on its own lists all pm parameters, and show pm-catalog <catalog-name> returns the same units and type pair. The parameter key is an identityref (pm parameter).

Yes: set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled. The global-data-supervision attribute exists specifically to enable PM data-supervision globally without having to toggle it individually. Its values are auto-enabled, which globally enables the PM data-supervision flag, and manual, which is the default and means the flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry. The pm-profile object holds information on all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. show pm-profile displays the current setting. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the per-resource-type defaults with pm-profile-entry, which configures PM per resource type: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true. default-data-supervision states whether newly created resources of this type have PM data supervision automatically enabled; the companion default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision. Both are true/false. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with a default of all, and location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with a default of all. show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> displays the current defaults. Note that a resource created before the change is unaffected; use pm-control-entry or pm-control for those.

Use show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset, for example show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9. The real-time-data-last-reset attribute is the date and time of the last real time data reset for that resource, and if the data was never reset it holds the date and time of the resource's creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string, 1..64 characters) and real-time-supervision (true/false, default true), and lists the pm-control-entry children such as pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end. To perform the reset itself use clear pm real-time, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, period, direction, location or AID.

Create a pm-threshold keyed on that exact instance: add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/errored-seconds high-threshold <value>, for example a key of the form <resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end/errored-seconds. The same key works with set to change it, show to read it back and delete to remove it. low-threshold and high-threshold accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na for not applicable, or not-supported, and both default to na. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with a default of all; location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with a default of all; period is the PM period, for example pm-15min or pm-24h. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use pm-threshold-profile, which holds the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type: show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter, while min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum values the parameter allows, so they bound what you may configure; low-threshold and high-threshold show what is currently configured. All six accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na, or not-supported. You write a new limit with set, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200.
